title: Medical trials are not the whole truth
subtitle: The potential and limitations of evidence-based medicine
author: Trisha Greenhalgh
introduction: We need to know whether drugs and other healthcare treatments work. The field of evidence-based medicine developed important tools, like randomised controlled trials, to do this. While they have helped drive huge advances in medical science, we should be cautious about relying solely on trials to evaluate new healthcare interventions. Although valuable, they can be misleading if badly designed, and they aren’t intrinsically superior to all other evidence. Evidence-based medicine should use real-life observations alongside trial data to get richer and more accurate answers for patients.
body:
If you had enough of a potentially life-saving drug for half the patients with a deadly disease but not enough for all of them, how would you decide whom to treat? Would you flip a coin? Allocate sequentially (patient 1 gets the treatment, patient 2 nothing, and so on)? Write ‘drug’ or ‘no drug’ on hundreds of cards, put them in identical sealed envelopes and shuffle thoroughly before picking? And what if the drug was possibly lifesaving but its benefits had not yet been proven? Might you use one of these allocation methods and a placebo group (who would get an inactive dummy pill) to test exactly how effective the drug was?

SUGGESTED VIEWING The medicine myth With Denis Noble, David Malone, Guy Brown, Nessa Carey

This was the dilemma faced in 1947 by a British statistician, Dr (later Sir)  Austin Bradford Hill, who was a stickler for methodology.  He had been concerned for some time that new drugs tended to be compared with placebos using either historical controls or sequential allocation. The former approach meant that one group of patients had received yesterday’s standard of care while those taking the active drug were getting today’s (hopefully better) standard in addition to the drug, making comparisons tricky. Sequential allocation was an improvement on this, but it meant that a doctor would know whether a patient was to get the active drug before deciding whether to put them in the trial. Misplaced compassion might nudge the doctor to tweak the allocation process—for example by re-ordering the patients or leaving sicker patients out of the trial altogether if they were in line for placebo. The results of such trials would suffer from bias—defined as anything that systematically distorts comparisons between groups. If an active treatment group contains sicker patients than the placebo group, the drug will appear less effective than it actually is.

Bradford Hill had written a series of articles in the medical journal The Lancet in 1937 arguing to replace historical controls and sequential allocation with some kind of concealed allocation (in his day, this was done by putting cards in sealed envelopes; these days we use computer-generated random numbers). But despite the soundness of Bradford Hill’s arguments, practice was slow to change.

SUGGESTED VIEWING How medicine ignores our bodies With David Healy

Then came the Second World War and its aftermath. The new antibiotic, streptomycin, was believed to be effective against pulmonary tuberculosis, which at the time killed approximately one person in 20 in the UK. But streptomycin was made in significant quantities only in the USA, where it was subject to tight export controls. The British Government managed to buy a small quantity of American streptomycin (enough for some but not all known tuberculosis patients) and passed it to the Medical Research Council (MRC). The MRC decided that a clinical trial led by Bradford Hill, with concealed allocation using sealed envelopes, was the fairest way of distributing the scarce drug and the most robust way of testing its efficacy. In that landmark trial, 15 of 55 patients in the control group but only four of 55 in the streptomycin group died in the first six months.

The MRC streptomycin trial was paradigm-shifting for two reasons. First, it demonstrated that streptomycin was an effective initial treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis (though as was later found, it wasn’t much use on its own in the longer term). And second, it established the randomised controlled trial (RCT) as the methodological gold standard for testing any drug against placebo (or another drug). This milestone marks, for some medical historians at least, the onset of what would later be dubbed the era of ‘evidence-based medicine’ (EBM).

Over the next few decades, RCTs of drugs and preventive therapies became commonplace. By comparing two groups that differed only in the treatment they were taking, it was possible to isolate out the benefits—and also any side effects—attributable to the active drug. The effectiveness of statins for reducing the risk of heart disease, chemotherapy for cancer and vaccines to protect against infectious diseases, for example, were established through RCTs—and also through combining the findings of several RCTs using the statistical technique of meta-analysis.

As the science of RCTs became more sophisticated, other kinds of bias—including performance bias (when the active drug group gets more frequent or more intensive monitoring than the placebo group), measurement bias (when doctors look more carefully for side effects, or are more likely to record these, if they know someone is taking the active drug), attrition bias (due to differences in how many participants withdraw from the study in each group) and publication bias (when a ‘positive’ study is more likely to be published than one showing no difference between the groups)—were identified and addressed. EBM enthusiasts have developed a smorgasbord of ‘risk of bias tools’—systematic ways of checking for these and other biases.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Morality, Hypocrisy and Health With Mary Ann Sieghart, Kevin Sabet, Mike Trace

It is simply not true that RCTs eliminate bias or that the findings of an RCT, however badly it has been done, are more trustworthy than those of a non-randomized study, however well done. But the more naïve members of the EBM movement can be like the child with a hammer to whom every problem is a nail. As she happily hammers the furniture, the cat and her breakfast egg, she closes her mind to the limitations of her favorite tool across a range of contexts.

RCTs have produced highly misleading findings when testing complex interventions—things like education or advice, new ways of organising services, or the use of digital technologies, all of which require humans to engage, learn stuff and act differently. Unless such interventions have been fully optimized (ensuring that the humans are maximally supported and incentivized to behave in the way intended, for example), any RCTs are likely to show weak or no effects.

A RCT undertaken across several sites in Scotland appeared to show that human support for women trying to breastfeed had no overall impact on breastfeeding rates. Indeed, in some sites, being in the ‘breastfeeding support’ group was associated with lower breastfeeding rates than being in the control group. Careful analysis of what was actually happening on the ground showed that in those sites, the intervention was not gentle, non-judgemental encouragement from an experienced support worker who had all the time in the world to help you get baby to latch on. Rather, it was a highly formalized set of advice delivered in unsuitable (cold, noisy, unwelcoming) premises by an overworked staff member working rigidly to a protocol. Leadership in those sites was weak, and the breastfeeding ‘support’ teams had low morale and (in some cases) little interest in, or commitment to, establishing breastfeeding in new moms. Small wonder that in these sites, being left alone to find your own support—perhaps from a sister or a neighbour, and in a way that worked for you—was more effective. But this commonsense interpretation didn’t stop some people concluding that it was now scientifically proven that breastfeeding support didn’t work.

In digital technology development, the standard research approach outside medicine is iterative design, in which an early prototype is progressively improved, first in a ‘living lab’ setting and then in real-world use cases using the ‘fail early, fail often’ principle. Agile designers make extensive use of methods like ethnography (carefully watching people use the product) and think-aloud techniques (in which the user voices their concerns and uncertainties while using the product).

Sadly, whilst these methods are also used to some extent to develop medical technologies, the product is often then tested against placebo in an RCT that is expensive, time-consuming and pointless (the version of the software tested in the trial will be out of date by the time the results are published). Did you ask for a RCT of your smartphone upgrade against the previous version before you installed it?  Of course not. I’m not saying that software never needs to be tested in experimental trials, but extrapolating the same ‘hierarchy of evidence’ that placed RCTs in pole position for drug research to fast-advancing digital tech is both impractical and illogical.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Doctors and the Danger Industry With David Healy

RCTs are often (wrongly) assumed to take the politics out of policymaking. If we know what works, policy decisions surely just need to ‘follow the science’? If only! Scientific findings (from RCTs as well as other study designs) are frequently ambiguous, incomplete, conflicting or contested. A drug or procedure might be effective but unaffordable by the patient or the healthcare provider. In publicly funded healthcare, the opportunity costs can loom large (my expensive heart drug means no hip replacement for you). It may be impossible to provide the treatment in certain settings—for example, if it requires a skilled professional to administer and there are no such people available. And some interventions (masks, opioid replacement or in-vitro fertilisation [IVF], for example) may be deemed unacceptable because of their perceived social and moral implications. All parties in policy debates tend to invoke ‘scientific evidence’—but which science gets placed on the table depends on the argument being made (e.g. take-home baby rates to boost pro-IVF arguments; surveys of evangelical Christians to boost anti-IVF arguments).

Bradford Hill’s name is often invoked by misguided EBM purists who seek to impose RCTs on every branch of medical and social research (not to mention policymaking). But the man credited with running the world’s first RCT is probably turning in his grave at the epistemic trespassing occurring in his name. Despite his visionary insights about the value of the RCT, Bradford Hill also firmly believed that this blunt, oversimplified experimental technique (which reduced a complex world to a study of A versus B) could only ever provide part of the evidence base for a real-world decision. He developed nine questions (known as the Bradford Hill criteria) which needed answering before concluding that a particular intervention caused a particular observed outcome. Some of those criteria require RCT evidence—but others require explanatory evidence about how the intervention might work, obtained from careful observation in real-world settings.

I suspect Bradford Hill would have been horrified that the method—RCTs—which he promoted in the 1930s for the rigorous testing of drugs has now become an indiscriminate hammer wielded by EBM zealots who seek to impose a hierarchy rather than a pluralism of evidence. To remain relevant in a complex and changing world, EBM needs to follow Bradford Hill’s original instructions and take a humbler, more pluralist approach to scientific evidence.
